interactive.title: Rates on linked graphs
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in twelve small screens with the slope tracker's linked graphs: two graphs, one above the other, sharing the same time across. The top graph shows an amount on the job. A point P can be dragged along it, the tangent at P rides with it, and the bottom graph drops a dot at the same time, as high as the tangent's slope. First comes charge passing a point in a cable, q coulombs after t seconds, with example rules. For q = 3t the dots sit on a flat line at 3 A, because an ampere is one coulomb each second; for q = 0.5t² they trace the line i = t, so 4 A at 4 s. Then a 0.01 F capacitor whose voltage climbs 5 V each second for 4 s and then holds at 20 V. Its bottom graph is the capacitance times the slope, i = C dv/dt: 50 mA while the voltage climbs, and 0 where it holds. Then a sketch, with no numbers on its axes, of a capacitor charging from a steady supply through a resistor, with a bracket from P up to the supply's voltage for what is left across the resistor: its voltage climbs steeply, then more and more gently, and the current below starts high and falls away towards zero. Then a 0.5 H coil, with its current on top and the voltage across it below, v = L di/dt: 2 V while the current climbs 4 A each second, 0 V while it holds, and −2 V while it falls 4 A each second. Then three graphs for motion: displacement s, how far along from the start, on top; velocity, its slope, in the middle; and acceleration, the slope of the velocity, at the bottom. The speeding boat, s = t² metres, has velocity 2t and a flat acceleration of 2. A trolley shoved up a ramp, s = 8t − t² metres, has velocity 8 − 2t, which crosses zero at 4 s while its acceleration stays at −2. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it: a puzzle offers three answers, and a wrong pick is shown going wrong on the graphs.
interactive.ignores: Every rule is an example, chosen so the numbers come out exactly. The capacitor's climb and the coil's current are drawn with sharp corners; a real voltage or current rounds each corner, so the current or voltage below changes quickly rather than all at once. The capacitor and coil are ideal parts: a real capacitor leaks a very little current at a steady voltage, and a real coil's resistance gives a small voltage at a steady current. The trolley's rule keeps its acceleration the same up and down; friction would make it a little different each way.

explain.text:
Read in its units, a derivative is a rate on the job: so much of one thing per unit of another, at one instant. Its unit is the top graph's unit per the unit across, and that unit tells you what it measures. Take charge. An ampere is one coulomb of charge passing a point each second,[^1][^2] so if 3 C pass every second, the graph of charge passed against time is a straight line climbing 3 C each second, and the current is 3 A: the slope of the charge graph, in coulombs per second. When the current changes, the same holds at each instant, using the tangent's slope: the current is the derivative of the charge that flows, with respect to time,[^3] written i = dq/dt. That is the dy/dx from lesson 2 with letters that say what is measured, q for charge and t for time; writing it this way is quite common in engineering and physics.[^4] Say the charge passed after t seconds is q = 0.5t² coulombs, an example rule. The power rule gives dq/dt = 0.5 × 2t = t, so at 4 s the current is 4 A. At that moment the charge graph stands at 0.5 × 16 = 8 C, and the chord from the start gives 8 ÷ 4 = 2 A on average. Neither is the current now: the height says how much charge has passed, the chord how fast on average, and the tangent's slope how fast at that instant.

A capacitor shows why the difference matters on the job. The charge on a capacitor is its capacitance times the voltage across it, q = Cv: one farad holds one coulomb for each volt.[^5] C is fixed, and a number in front stays when you differentiate,[^6] so i = dq/dt = C dv/dt: the current through a capacitor is its capacitance times the slope of its voltage graph.[^7] The units agree: q = Cv makes a farad a coulomb per volt, so farads times volts per second are coulombs per second, which is amps. So it is not how high the voltage is that sets the current, but how fast it is changing.[^7] Make the voltage on a 0.01 F capacitor climb a steady 5 V each second and the current is 0.01 × 5 = 0.05 A, 50 mA, the whole time it climbs. Hold the voltage at 20 V and its slope is 0, so the current is 0, however high it is held. Across the same resistor, a higher voltage means more current; for a capacitor, it is the change of voltage that drives the current. Now charge a capacitor from a steady supply through a resistor. The resistor has the supply's voltage less the capacitor's across it, so at the start, with the capacitor uncharged, the most current flows, and by i = C dv/dt the voltage climbs fastest. As the capacitor's voltage climbs, less is left across the resistor, so less current flows and the voltage climbs more slowly. So the voltage climbs quickly at first, then more and more slowly as it nears the supply's voltage, and the current is largest at the start, when the voltage is lowest, and falls away towards zero as the voltage levels off.[^3] A coil, an inductor, has the same pattern with voltage and current swapped: the voltage across it is the derivative of its current, its inductance times how fast the current changes,[^8] v = L di/dt. A steady current makes no voltage across it, and a current that falls fast makes a large voltage, the other way round to the one a rising current makes. These capacitor and coil rules are for ideal parts, a simplified picture: a real capacitor leaks a very little current at a steady voltage, and a real coil's resistance gives a small voltage at a steady current.

Motion works the same way and adds a second step. Measure displacement, s, as how far something is from a starting point along its path, plus one way and minus the other. Differentiate it with respect to time and you get its [[velocity]] at that time,[^9] its speed with a sign for its direction, in metres per second. Velocity changes too, and its rate of change, in metres per second each second, is the [[acceleration]]; the Second Engineer syllabus asks for both, velocity from displacement and acceleration from velocity.[^10] Acceleration is a derivative of a derivative, the [[second derivative]] of displacement, which textbooks write d²s/dt². The speeding boat, s = t² metres, has velocity 2t and acceleration 2 m per s each second, the same at every moment. Now shove a trolley up a long ramp, with s = 8t − t² metres up the ramp as an example rule. Its velocity is 8 − 2t and its acceleration −2. At 4 s it is 16 m up and its velocity is 0: it has stopped for an instant. Its acceleration is still −2, because its velocity is still falling, from going up to coming down, so a velocity of zero does not mean an acceleration of zero. Anything holding steady, a charge, a voltage, a position, has a rate of 0, because the derivative of a constant is zero.[^11] **Read a derivative in its units, so much per so much: current is how fast charge flows, i = dq/dt,[^3] a capacitor's current is its capacitance times how fast its voltage changes,[^7] and velocity is how fast displacement changes, with acceleration how fast velocity changes.[^9][^10]**

analogy.text: Picture filling a straight-sided header tank with nothing drawn off. The flow in is the tank's floor area times how fast the water level rises. A tank holding a steady level takes no flow at all, however high the level stands, and a level rising fast means a big flow, even near the bottom. A capacitor follows the same rule, with its voltage as the level, its capacitance as the floor area and its current as the flow: i = C dv/dt.
analogy.breaks: Water piles up inside a tank, but charge does not pile up inside a capacitor: as much current leaves by one lead as arrives by the other, while one plate gains charge and the other loses the same amount. And the push a tank's level gives comes from the water's weight, while a capacitor's voltage comes from the charge separated between its plates.

practice.text:
- Name the two things: the amount that changes (charge, voltage, current, displacement) and what it changes with, usually time.
- Write the amount as a rule in time and differentiate it term by term with the power rule.
- Give the answer the top unit per the unit across: coulombs per second is amps; metres per second; volts per second.
- Multiply by the part's own number where the job's rule has one: C for a capacitor's current, L for a coil's voltage.
- Put in the moment you want. A minus sign means falling: charge flowing back, a voltage the other way round, motion the minus way along its path.
- For acceleration, differentiate a second time.
- Check with a chord over a small step: its slope should be just off your answer.

**Rules of thumb:** the height says how much, the slope says how fast. Anything holding steady has a rate of 0. A capacitor's current and a coil's voltage follow change, not size.

**Worked example:** Say a 0.002 F (2,000 µF) capacitor has its voltage raised by the rule v = 4t² volts after t seconds, an example rule. Then dv/dt = 8t volts per second, and at 1.5 s that is 12 V per s. So i = C dv/dt = 0.002 × 12 = 0.024 A, 24 mA. Check with a chord: at 1.5 s the voltage is 9 V and at 1.6 s it is 4 × 1.6² = 10.24 V, so the chord's slope is 1.24 ÷ 0.1 = 12.4 V per s, giving 24.8 mA, just above.

**Common mistakes**
- Reading the height as the rate: at 1.5 s the voltage is 9 V, but 0.002 × 9 = 0.018 A is not the current.
- Using the average since the start: 9 V in 1.5 s is 6 V per s, half the slope at 1.5 s.
- Dropping C or L: the voltage's slope alone is in volts per second, not amps.
- Taking a velocity of zero to mean no acceleration: the trolley at the top of its ramp is still accelerating at −2 m per s each second.

interactive.html:
Linked graphs sharing one time across: above, an amount on the job; below, what its slope gives at each moment.

Every rule is an example and every dot is worked out from it; the charging curve is only a sketch.

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the current dot below following the voltage graph's slope, not its height, dropping to zero where the voltage holds steady, when you drag the point along a capacitor's voltage graph.

checks.label: The instantaneous current is the time derivative of the charge that flows: on every charge screen each dot below sits straight under its time, as high as the slope the chords there settle on from either side, and the tangent through P has that slope
One ampere is the current in which one coulomb of charge passes a point each second: the charge line climbing 3 C every second drops every dot at 3 A, wherever P goes

The current through a capacitor is equal to the capacitance times the slope of its voltage graph: on every capacitor screen each dot below reads 0.01 F × that slope, in mA, so 50 mA while the voltage climbs 5 V each second and 0 while it holds

Velocity from the displacement-time function and acceleration from the velocity-time function: on both motion screens the middle dots read the slope of the displacement graph (2t for the boat, 8 − 2t for the trolley) and the bottom dots the slope of the velocity graph (2, then −2)

The derivative of a constant function is zero: wherever a voltage or a current holds steady (the capacitor at 20 V and at 50 V, the coil at 8 A, the coil before and after the switch-off) its rate below is 0

Charging through a resistor (the sketch): the charge, and so the voltage, climbs at every step but stays under the supply's voltage, and the current below falls at every step towards zero, largest at the start and nearly 0 by the end; the bracket for what is left across the resistor shrinks as P climbs

The voltage across a coil is the derivative of its current, times its inductance: on both coil screens each dot below reads 0.5 H × the slope of the current graph, so 2 V while it climbs 4 A each second, 0 while it holds, −2 V while it falls and −100 V switched off

From the rules, by hand: 3t gives 3 A; 0.5t² at 4 s is 8 C, slope 4, chord 8 ÷ 4 = 2; the capacitor climbing 5 V per s gives 0.01 × 5 = 0.05 A = 50 mA, and 0 held at 20 V or 50 V (0.01 × 50 = 0.5); the coil gives 0.5 × 4 = 2 V, 0 and −2 V; switched off, −2 ÷ 0.01 = −200 A per s and −100 V (0.5 × 2 = 1); the boat at 3 s is 9 m, 6 m per s, 2; the trolley at 4 s is 16 m, 0, −2; 2t² + 3t at 2 s is 14 C and 11 A (19 with the power kept); t² volts at 3 s is 9 V, slope 6, 60 mA (90 from the height); and the screens' words quote these values

Every puzzle offers three different answers and accepts only the right one; each wrong answer is the slip it stands for: 8 A and 2 A against 4 A; 0.5 A and 50 mA against 0 A; the end and the same all along against the start; 1 V and 0 V against −100 V; 0 and 16 against −2; 14 A and 19 A against 11 A; 90 mA and 6 A against 60 mA

Before an answer no puzzle shows it: no tangent, no dot on the answer's graph, nothing red, and the working ends in a question mark; a right answer shows its value with nothing red, and every wrong answer shows its slip in red
Dragging P keeps it on a half second inside the axes and never on a corner of the capacitor's or the coil's graph, and the dots below skip the corners
Every demonstration has finished arriving within 5 s of its screen opening, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; every answer's motion, right or wrong, within 1.3 s

applied.problem: 'A minus sign means ... motion back towards the start' is not always true: with displacement signed, a negative velocity on the minus side of the start moves away from it; a minus velocity means motion the minus way.
A header tank in use is drawn from while held at a steady level, so 'a steady level takes no flow at all' is only true with nothing drawn off; the flow-in rule likewise needs no outflow.
A tank's level does not come from the water's weight (it comes from how much water is stored); it is the pressure the level gives that comes from the weight, the thing compared with voltage.

The coil screen also has sharp corners (current climbs, holds, falls), so its voltage jumps 2 V, 0 V, -2 V at once; a real coil's current rounds those corners too, which ignores only says of the capacitor.
